concepts.title: Classifying Carbohydrates and Sugars
concepts.definition: Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or anything that hydrolyses into such units; they sort by hydrolysis behaviour into monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and by reactivity into reducing sugars (free aldehyde or keto group, Tollens and Fehling positive) versus non-reducing ones with those groups locked up.
concepts.key_idea: The Cx(H2O)y formula is only a rough guide: acetic acid fits it without being a carbohydrate, and rhamnose is one without fitting it.
question_patterns: classify ribose, maltose, galactose, fructose and lactose as monosaccharides or disaccharides
define carbohydrates in terms of their functional groups rather than the hydrate formula
what distinguishes a reducing sugar from a non-reducing one
why is sucrose called a non-sugar while glucose is a sugar
name the monosaccharides released when sucrose and maltose each hydrolyse
sort starch, cellulose and glycogen into the right carbohydrate class

solution_steps.explain: no further hydrolysis means monosaccharide; two to ten units oligosaccharide; many units polysaccharide
a free aldehydic or ketonic group reduces Tollens and Fehling reagents, tagging the sugar as reducing

concepts.title: Open-Chain Structure Evidence for Glucose
concepts.definition: Five reactions pin glucose as a straight-chain aldohexose: heating with HI unrolls it to n-hexane, oxime and cyanohydrin formation exposes a carbonyl, bromine water stops at gluconic acid proving the carbonyl is an aldehyde, acetic anhydride delivers a pentaacetate counting five OH groups, and nitric acid drags both glucose and gluconic acid to saccharic acid revealing a terminal primary alcohol.
concepts.key_idea: Each reagent interrogates one structural claim, and together they build the CHO-CHOH chain without any instrument at all.
question_patterns: what does glucose form on prolonged heating with HI and what does it prove

explain how the pentaacetate derivative fixes the number of OH groups in glucose

list the reactions that establish glucose as an aldohexose with a straight chain

solution_steps.explain: HI tests the carbon skeleton, hydroxylamine and HCN the carbonyl, bromine water the aldehyde choice
pentaacetate counts OH groups and saccharic acid exposes the CH2OH at carbon one

concepts.title: Cyclic Hemiacetal Forms, Anomers and Furanose Fructose
concepts.definition: Glucose refuses Schiff's test, skips the bisulphite adduct and crystallises in two forms, so the CHO of C1 must cyclise with the C5 hydroxyl into a six-membered pyranose hemiacetal; the two configurations at the new anomeric carbon are the alpha and beta anomers, while fructose builds a five-membered furanose ring the same way from its C2 keto group.
concepts.key_idea: Open-chain and both cyclic forms sit in equilibrium in solution, which is why glucose misses some aldehyde reactions yet still reduces Tollens reagent.
question_patterns: why does glucose fail to give Schiff's test despite carrying an aldehyde group
explain the two crystalline forms of glucose and the ring size of each
define the anomeric carbon and name the pair of isomers it creates
which hydroxyl group closes the pyranose ring of glucose
how does fructose build its five-membered furanose ring
why does the pentaacetate of glucose ignore hydroxylamine

solution_steps.explain: the C5 OH adds to the C1 aldehyde forming a hemiacetal, hiding the free CHO
the two arrangements of the new OH define the alpha and beta anomers in pyranose or furanose rings

concepts.title: Glycosidic Linkage in Disaccharides
concepts.definition: Two monosaccharides weld together through an oxygen bridge left when water departs, the glycosidic linkage; sucrose locks C1 of alpha-glucose to C2 of beta-fructose and so cannot reduce, while maltose (C1-C4 of two glucoses) and lactose (C1 of galactose to C4 of glucose) keep a free aldehyde available and reduce.
concepts.key_idea: Whether the reducing groups take part in the linkage decides the sugar class: tied carbonyl means non-reducing, free carbonyl means reducing.
question_patterns: define the glycosidic linkage and name the atoms it joins

which carbons of which units does the sucrose linkage connect
predict the expected products when lactose is hydrolysed

solution_steps.explain: the glycosidic bond names the two anomeric or carrier carbons it spans
an unbound aldehydic or ketonic group keeps the sugar reducing

concepts.title: Invert Sugar Net Rotation after Sucrose Hydrolysis
concepts.definition: Sucrose rotates light dextrorotatory but its hydrolysis frees dextro glucose and laevo fructose, and since the fructose twist outweighs the glucose one the mixture ends laevorotatory; adding the two signed rotations gives the net reading, and the sign flip from plus to minus is why the product is called invert sugar.
concepts.key_idea: Fructose at about -92.4 degrees beats glucose at about +52.5 degrees, so hydrolysis turns the sign of rotation negative.
question_patterns: glucose contributes +52.5 degrees and fructose -92.4 degrees; find the net rotation of the hydrolysis mixture
calculate the overall rotation after complete hydrolysis of sucrose from the two monosaccharide rotations

solution_steps.explain: equal moles of the two monosaccharides contribute their rotations algebraically

concepts.title: Storage and Structural Polysaccharides
concepts.definition: Starch stores energy in plants as a mix of water-soluble unbranched amylose (about 15-20 percent) and insoluble branched amylopectin (about 80-85 percent) both built from alpha-glucose, cellulose stretches as a straight beta-glucose chain in plant cell walls, and glycogen plays the animal starch role in liver and muscle with even heavier branching.
concepts.key_idea: The alpha versus beta glucose choice decides everything: alpha builds digestible starch and glycogen, beta builds cellulose that humans cannot digest.

solution_steps.explain: alpha-glucose polymers store fuel while beta-glucose chains build walls
C1-C4 links extend chains and C1-C6 links throw branches in amylopectin and glycogen

concepts.title: Amino Acids: Zwitter Ions and Classification
concepts.definition: Alpha amino acids carry NH2 and COOH on the same carbon, and in water the acid end donates its proton to the basic end, building a dipolar zwitter ion that reacts with both acids and bases; equal group counts make them neutral, extra amino groups basic, extra carboxyl groups acidic, and the ten the body cannot build are the essential dietary ones.
concepts.key_idea: Except glycine every natural alpha amino acid is optically active, and the L form with NH2 drawn on the left dominates nature.
question_patterns: explain the amphoteric behaviour of amino acids in aqueous solution

solution_steps.action: let the groups talk to each other
solution_steps.explain: intramolecular proton transfer from COOH to NH2 gives the dipolar ion
the balance sorts the acid as neutral, basic or acidic; diet sorts it as essential or not

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds and the Four Protein Structure Levels
concepts.definition: The COOH of one amino acid condenses with the NH2 of the next, shedding water and forming the amide-like peptide bond -CO-NH-; chains fold first into alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheets (secondary), then into the overall fibrous or globular shape (tertiary), and several chains pack as sub-units (quaternary), all held by hydrogen bonds, disulphide links, van der Waals and electrostatic forces.
concepts.key_idea: Heat or pH change denatures a protein by uncoiling secondary and tertiary structure while the primary sequence survives, as when egg white sets on boiling.
question_patterns: define the peptide linkage and name the small molecule lost when it forms

solution_steps.action: condense the acid end with the amine end
solution_steps.explain: each peptide bond is an amide built by eliminating one water molecule
sequence, then helix or sheet, then overall shape, then sub-unit assembly

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds in a Polypeptide Chain
concepts.definition: Each new amino acid added to a chain costs exactly one peptide linkage, so a chain of n residues holds n minus 1 peptide bonds; the tripeptide case states it directly with three residues joined by two linkages.
concepts.key_idea: Insulin with 51 residues therefore hides 50 peptide bonds, and the polypeptide-versus-protein boundary near a hundred residues is a soft one.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech205.txt section 10.2.3, dipeptide to protein chain counting (lines ~707-722)

solution_steps.action: subtract one from the residue count
solution_steps.explain: every extra residue beyond the first adds exactly one peptide bond

concepts.title: Enzymes as Specific Biocatalysts
concepts.definition: Enzymes are mostly globular proteins that run body chemistry under mild conditions, name themselves after their substrate or reaction with an -ase ending, accept only fitting substrates, and work by cutting the activation energy barrier the way chemical catalysts do.
concepts.key_idea: Maltase hydrolysing maltose to glucose shows both habits: substrate-derived name and single-reaction specificity.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech205.txt section 10.3 with mechanism of enzyme action (lines ~829-862)
question_patterns: what does the ending -ase signal in an enzyme name

solution_steps.action: read the name for the job
solution_steps.explain: substrate plus -ase (maltase) or reaction class plus -ase (oxidoreductase) tells the catalytic task
the enzyme offers a surface that needs far less activation energy than the uncatalysed route

concepts.title: Enzyme Catalysis Activation Energy Saving
concepts.definition: Sucrose hydrolyses with acid behind a 6.22 kJ per mol barrier but sucrase drops the barrier to 2.15 kJ per mol, so the enzyme's saving is the difference of the two barriers expressed as a percentage of the uncatalysed one.
concepts.key_idea: Even a small absolute drop in activation energy accelerates a reaction enormously, which is how tiny enzyme quantities suffice.
concepts.textbook_ref: lech205.txt section 10.3.1, sucrose activation energy figures (lines ~857-862)
question_patterns: acid hydrolysis of sucrose needs 6.22 kJ per mol and sucrase needs 2.15; calculate the percent drop in activation energy

solution_steps.explain: the absolute saving is the uncatalysed barrier minus the enzyme barrier
dividing by the original barrier and multiplying by 100 gives the percent drop

concepts.title: Fat-Soluble versus Water-Soluble Vitamins
concepts.definition: Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fats, lodge in liver and adipose tissue and so build up, while the B group plus vitamin C dissolve in water, wash out in urine and need regular refills (B12 excepted); shortfalls bring signature diseases such as xerophthalmia for A, beri-beri for B1, scurvy for C, rickets for D and slow clotting for K.
concepts.key_idea: Vitamin C cannot be stored because water carries it away, which is why citrus fruit must keep arriving in the diet.

solution_steps.explain: fat-soluble A, D, E, K store; water-soluble B group and C flush out

concepts.title: Nucleosides, Nucleotides and the Nucleic Acid Backbone
concepts.definition: Full hydrolysis of DNA or RNA frees a pentose sugar, phosphoric acid and nitrogen bases; a base clipped onto the 1-prime carbon of the sugar is a nucleoside, phosphorylation at the 5-prime carbon upgrades it to a nucleotide, and phosphodiester links between 5-prime and 3-prime carbons chain the nucleotides into the polynucleotide.
concepts.key_idea: DNA carries the sugar 2-deoxyribose while RNA carries ribose, and thymine appears only in DNA as uracil does only in RNA.

solution_steps.explain: base plus sugar makes the nucleoside; adding phosphate at 5-prime makes the nucleotide
the phosphodiester bridge alternates sugar and phosphate down the strand with bases hanging off

concepts.title: DNA versus RNA: Strands, Pairing and Roles
concepts.definition: Watson and Crick's DNA is a double helix whose strands pair adenine with thymine and cytosine with guanine through hydrogen bonds, making the strands complementary rather than identical; RNA runs single-stranded, sometimes folding back on itself, and splits its labour among messenger, ribosomal and transfer RNAs that execute the protein synthesis DNA encodes.
concepts.key_idea: DNA stores and duplicates heredity while the three RNA species translate that store into proteins, and base-sequence uniqueness makes DNA fingerprinting possible.
question_patterns: why are the two strands of DNA called complementary rather than identical

solution_steps.explain: A-T and C-G hydrogen bonding locks the double helix while RNA pairs A-U when it folds
DNA archives the message; mRNA carries it, rRNA builds the site, tRNA ferries amino acids

concepts.title: Hormones as Intercellular Messengers
concepts.definition: Endocrine glands pour hormones straight into the blood to steer distant targets; they arrive as steroids such as oestrogens and androgens, polypeptides such as insulin, or amino-acid derivatives such as epinephrine, and pairs like insulin with glucagon hold blood glucose inside narrow limits while thyroxine, an iodinated tyrosine derivative, sets the metabolic pace.
concepts.key_idea: Dietary iodine shortage swells the thyroid as hypothyroidism sets in, which is why table salt gets iodised.
question_patterns: how do insulin and glucagon cooperate to hold blood sugar steady

solution_steps.explain: gland to blood to target cell defines a hormone, whatever its chemistry
insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose; excess or deficit of thyroxine flips the metabolic state
